title: Groundtruth Desk Scan
one_liner: Uses AI agents to scan public LiDAR and satellite data for possible archaeological features before a project breaks ground.
speaker: Peter Diamandis
context: A non-archaeologist set dozens of AI agents loose on public NASA LiDAR overnight. They flagged a possible unmapped Maya site, which Mexican officials said looks like a new find. Alex says archaeology is about to be 'cooked'.
customer: US cultural resource management (CRM) consulting firms, plus the solar, wind and transmission developers that pay for their Phase I desk reviews
problem: Before fieldwork, someone has to go through huge areas of LiDAR hillshade by hand looking for mounds, platforms and old earthworks. It is slow and expensive, and when a site is missed late, construction gets delayed.
revenue_model: Per-project desk scan, about $1,500–$5,000 per site footprint, depending on area (estimate). A white-label subscription for CRM firms at about $500 a month (estimate).
why_now: The episode describes 48 agents reviewing 1,200 square kilometres of public LiDAR overnight with no specialist model. It also covers the launch of a natural-language search over a decade of daily satellite imagery.
first_steps: Download free USGS 3DEP LiDAR for one county where a solar project has been announced, run an AI-assisted hillshade review, and write up a sample anomaly report
Send the sample report to 10 CRM firm principals and ask what they currently pay for desk-based assessment hours
Offer one firm a free scan of a project they have already surveyed, so you can measure hits and misses against their field results
cost_to_start: About 2–3 weeks and under $500 for compute and model usage (estimate)
competition: In-house GIS staff at CRM firms, academic LiDAR-survey groups and general geospatial AI vendors. A cheap service built only for pre-construction desk scans is probably rare.
risks: False positives could erode trust. Site locations are sensitive, so reports have to stay confidential. A professional archaeologist still has to sign off, so the service supports CRM firms but cannot replace them. LiDAR coverage is uneven.

tool.title: Hillshade Hunter
tool.one_liner: Upload a LiDAR elevation tile and get a ranked list of candidate mounds, platforms and linear earthworks.
tool.demo: The user uploads an elevation grid (ASCII grid or a GeoTIFF exported as a PNG height map). The page renders a multi-angle hillshade, runs local-relief and flatness filters, and outlines candidate flat platforms and raised features with size estimates. It then exports a CSV and a printable anomaly sheet for a desk review.
tool.data_plan: The customer's own LiDAR tile, which they can download free from public sources like USGS 3DEP. A bundled synthetic sample tile powers example mode. All processing runs in the browser.
acceptance: Loading the bundled sample tile draws a hillshade and outlines at least 3 candidate features, each with an ID
Moving the relief-threshold slider changes the number of outlined candidates and updates the ranked table
Clicking a row in the candidate table highlights that feature on the map and shows its estimated width and height
Clicking export downloads a CSV with candidate ID, pixel location, size and score
The sample tile is clearly labelled as synthetic example data
